draft.title: Solving quadratics by factorising
card: A quadratic equation has an \(x^{2}\) term. To solve it by factorising, first move every term to one side so the other side is 0.
Factorise the quadratic into two brackets. For \(x^{2} + bx + c\), find two numbers that multiply to \(c\) and add to \(b\).
This is the null factor law: if two things multiply to give 0, at least one of them must be 0. So set each bracket equal to 0 and solve each one.
Example: \(x^{2} - x = 6\). Subtract 6 to get \(x^{2} - x - 6 = 0\). The numbers \(-3\) and 2 multiply to \(-6\) and add to \(-1\). So \((x - 3)(x + 2) = 0\), which gives \(x = 3\) or \(x = -2\).
draft.remember: Get 0 on one side, factorise, then use the null factor law.

a.q: Use the null factor law on \((x - 4)(x + 1) = 0\). What are the solutions?
a.why: Set each bracket to 0: \(x - 4 = 0\) gives \(x = 4\), and \(x + 1 = 0\) gives \(x = -1\). Taking the numbers in the brackets as the answers gives the wrong signs.

b.q: Priya solves \(x^{2} + 2x - 15 = 0\) by factorising. Which are her solutions?
b.why: The numbers 5 and \(-3\) multiply to \(-15\) and add to 2, so \((x + 5)(x - 3) = 0\). That gives \(x = -5\) or \(x = 3\). The option \(x = -3\) or \(x = 5\) comes from \((x + 3)(x - 5)\), but its matching numbers 3 and \(-5\) add to \(-2\), not 2.
b.clue: Find two numbers that multiply to \(-15\) and add to \(+2\).
